video.title: EP 565 Make Money Online With a Micro App | Validate Before Building

summary: Dark Horse Entrepreneur episode 565 argues that AI makes building apps fast but does not create demand, so aspiring micro-app founders should validate before building. It settles the 'validate vs copy an existing app' debate by saying existing apps prove a market but not that anyone will buy from you. It lays out a five-step test: micro-problem filter, proof checklist, switch conversation, smallest paid promise (pre-sale, do-it-by-hand, or specific waitlist), and a pre-set build/don't-build pass mark. The only worked example is a hypothetical $5/month game-day confirmation tool for youth cheer coaches.

speakers.name: Dark Horse Entrepreneur host (name not stated)
speakers.description: Podcaster since 2007, solo episode; mentions a daughter who did cheer for about a decade

ideas.name: Cheer coach game-day confirmation micro SaaS (illustrative)
ideas.one_liner: A single-feature app letting youth cheer coaches send one message and see which parents confirmed for game day, at $5/month.
ideas.customer: Youth cheer coaches juggling about 12 parents at a time
ideas.problem: Coaches chase each parent manually to confirm game-day attendance
ideas.offer: One message out, one view of who has confirmed; one feature only

pricing.notes: Illustrative example; 100 customers would equal $500 MRR (hypothetical).

acquisition_channels.details: Find coaches in Reddit, Facebook groups and niche forums; ask questions rather than pitch, respect group no-promotion rules; then invite to a chat.
One-page pre-sale site with promise, mock-up, price and Stripe buy button, or a specific waitlist ('early access to the coaches game day tool at the founding price').

ideas.delivery: Software app built after validation using AI tools (ChatGPT, Lovable, bolt.new, Cursor, Claude); before build, the founder manually texts parents and sends confirmation lists as a paid test.
ideas.startup_cost: not stated (a couple of evenings of validation)
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Pass mark example: three strangers pay or commit within 2 weeks

acquisition.how: Community research and interview requests are human-led (conversations are essential); landing page and waitlist can be automated, but posting in groups must respect rules and cold DMs to individuals are restricted under PECR.

onboarding.how: Self-serve signup and Stripe billing for a one-feature app can run unattended.

delivery.how: Once built, a simple scheduling/confirmation app is software; messaging features add some maintenance.

support.how: AI support agent handles routine questions with occasional human review.

uk_applicability.notes: Works in the UK with changes: youth cheer/sports clubs exist, but SMS to parents needs GDPR/PECR consent and child-data care. Pricing would be in GBP.

risks: Nobody may pay at $5/month; churn risk
Parent contact data and children's data bring GDPR obligations
Existing team-management apps may already cover this

tactics.name: Micro-problem filter (5 questions, pass at least 4)
steps: Who exactly has it (job title or situation)?
How often does it occur (weekly or better)?
What does it cost them now (time, money, embarrassment, missed sales)?
Are they already paying something to handle it?
Can one feature fix the core?
Fill in: 'I want to build an app that does X to solve Y problem for these users'

quote.text: If your fix needs 10 features, it's not a micro app. You need to shrink it
quote.speaker: Host

tactics.name: Proof checklist (need 3 or more)
steps: Find paid competitors in app stores and Product Hunt; check reviews and ratings
Search Reddit, Facebook groups and niche forums for unprompted complaints
Read competitors' one-star and three-star reviews for gaps
Google '[competitor] alternative' to find people looking to switch
Look for homemade workarounds like spreadsheets or templates
Copy exact customer quotes into a doc unedited for use on the sales page

tactics.name: Switch conversation interviews
steps: Find 5 to 10 people matching the buyer persona in the communities where complaints appeared
Ask questions rather than pitch, and follow group rules
Ask about the past: 'Walk me through the last time this happened'
Ask what they use now, what they hate, what they tried that failed, and what would make them switch
Never ask 'Would you use my app?'
Listen for heat and existing spend

quote.text: The question that's missing is, "Would you use my app?" Please never ask that.
quote.speaker: Host

tactics.name: Smallest paid promise test
steps: Write one sentence: 'I help this person do this one thing without this pain for this price'
Option 1 pre-sale: one-page site, mock-up, price, Stripe buy button, ship date and money-back guarantee
Option 2 do-it-by-hand: deliver the result manually for a small fee for a few weeks
Option 3 specific waitlist with founding price
Write the pass mark on a sticky note before starting
After 2 weeks, build if the mark is hit; otherwise change one variable (price, persona, feature) and retest or drop it

quote.text: If nobody will pay you to do it by hand, they probably won't pay for your software that does it, either.
quote.speaker: Host

tactics.name: 15-minute competitor review mining
steps: Pick your app idea
Find the biggest existing competitor
Read 20 one-star and three-star reviews
Copy lines that make you think 'I can fix that'

tools_mentioned.name: ChatGPT
tools_mentioned.purpose: Brainstorm recurring problems and generate code

warnings.warning: Proving a market exists is not the same as proving anyone will buy from you; you need a reason to switch.

quote.text: Proving a market exists is not the same as proving anybody will buy from you.
quote.speaker: Host

warnings.warning: Do not ask 'would you use my app?'; people say yes because it costs them nothing.
Zero competitors and zero complaints usually means an empty road for a reason, not an open lane.
Set the pass mark before testing, or you will grade on a curve and move the goalposts.
Honour the refund if a pre-sale app does not ship; reputation cannot be rebuilt by AI.
Treat YouTubers' income claims as their story, not your forecast; avoid gaming votes or buying fake downloads.
Do not pitch in communities that ban promotion; ask questions instead.

lessons.lesson: AI made building cheap but customer attention and your evenings are still scarce, so validate before building.

quote.text: Code got cheap. Your evenings, they didn't get cheap.
quote.speaker: Host

lessons.lesson: Existing paying competitors are evidence of a market, but you still need a specific reason for someone to switch.
Prefer evidence that cost people something (money, time, effort) over compliments or opinions.
Pre-commit to a numeric pass/fail threshold and deadline before running a test.
Ask about past behaviour, not future intentions, to get truthful customer answers.
Shrink offers to one feature for one specific person; vague 'help small businesses' ideas are too big.
Use AI as a brainstorming and sparring partner, but it cannot replace real customers.

quote.text: AI drafts but a human decides and you're the human.
quote.speaker: Host

lessons.lesson: Walking away after a two-week test is a cheap success, not failure; log what you learned each time.
Use customers' unedited words from complaints and reviews to write sales copy.

evidence_quality.rationale: Advisory, framework-style content with no first-hand revenue figures; the only numbers are hypothetical or second-hand (a $5 x 100 example and a 37-minute build story). The framework is sensible but unproven in the transcript.
evidence_quality.promotional_conflict: Host promotes a free micro app validation checklist and sells/grows newsletters (AI Escape Plan, Dark Horse Insider) at darkhorseentrepreneur.com and darkhorseinsider.com.
